title: Only comfort
hook: the Heidelberg Catechism begins: what is your only comfort in life and death?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luther's barber: four strands woven through one commandment, and a mind kept on the razor. Your line was a simple way to pray. Did a minute of whole attention find you? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-eight.

What is your only comfort in life and in death? That's the very first question of a catechism, a book of questions and answers for teaching the faith. It doesn't open with the nature of God or the order of the universe. It opens with the question someone asks at a sickbed, or lying awake in the small hours. The book is the Heidelberg Catechism, named for the German city it came from, and still taught in some Reformed churches. Some people learn its first answer by heart and carry it for life. Today: only comfort.

Here's the answer, put plainly. That I am not my own. That I belong, body and soul, in life and in death, to my faithful Savior Jesus Christ. It goes on: he has paid for my sins and set me free; he watches over me so that not a hair can fall from my head without the Father's will; and by his Spirit he makes me willing and ready to live for him. Notice what comfort means here. Not a mood. Not a cozy feeling that comes and goes. It's a fact about belonging: whose you are. And it starts with a negative: not my own. That line comes close to Paul's own words: "ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price." To some ears, not my own sounds like a loss. The catechism hears it as relief. On its terms, if I am not my own, I don't have to hold myself together. Someone faithful is holding me. Paul says it again to the Romans: "whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord's." Living and dying, both covered. And the line about the hairs of your head echoes Jesus in Matthew: "But the very hairs of your head are all numbered." Then the second question asks what you need to know to live and die in this comfort, and it answers in three parts: how great my sin and misery are, how I am set free from them, and how I am to thank God for that freedom. Guilt, grace and gratitude, as some teachers put it, and the rest of the catechism follows that order. Other churches have their own catechisms with their own first questions; Luther wrote a small one too. Heidelberg chose to begin with comfort.
screen: `WHETHER WE LIVE OR DIE, THE LORD'S.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with the question. Breathe slowly. Ask it of yourself, honestly: what is my comfort, in life and in death? Don't hurry to a right answer, or to any answer. Notice what comes up first: a person, a place, a habit, a hope, a blank. Let it be what it is. If you pray, you can set the catechism's line, I am not my own, beside whatever came up, and see how they sit together. If you don't, simply stay with the question. The bell holds the time.
Only comfort. The Heidelberg Catechism's first question, and its answer: I am not my own, but belong to my faithful Savior, in life and in death.
Your line: my only comfort. Today, when something shakes you, a headline, a phone call, a bill, ask the question once, quietly: what's my comfort here? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: In Reformed churches that use the Heidelberg Catechism, it is taught to young people and new members, and some congregations preach through it in sections called Lord's Days over the course of a year.

notes: The opening question is given in the hook without quotation marks: the English is a paraphrase (source marked quoted: null), not any particular translation.
The date in the index hook (1563) is not stated under the claims rule; the file's hook line drops it.
'Written for the Reformed churches of a German territory called the Palatinate' and 'taught in Reformed churches to this day': standard history; confirm wording.

Q1 answer paraphrased (belonging body and soul; paid for sins; set free; not a hair falls without the Father's will; Spirit makes me willing and ready to live for him). Q2's three parts (misery, deliverance, gratitude) and the catechism's three-part structure; confirm.
'Guilt, grace and gratitude, as some teachers put it' is attributed as a teaching summary.
'Luther wrote a small one too' refers to the Small Catechism; no ranking intended.
